content:
An environment once considered hostile to life’s chemistry

The surface of Venus reaches approximately 860°F under an atmospheric pressure 93 times greater than Earth’s, rendering ground conditions inhospitable to any known biology. High above that furnace, droplets in the cloud deck, 30 to 40 miles up present milder temperatures alongside near-pure sulfuric acid. Because meteorites regularly deliver organic peptides into the upper atmosphere, planetary scientists have debated whether those building blocks disintegrate on contact or persist inside the cloud layer.

MIT chemistry professor Mei Hong co-led the study with Professor of Planetary Sciences, Sara Seager, publishing their findings in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

How researchers tested peptide survival

Using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy to track molecular structure in high resolution, Hong’s team monitored three short peptides suspended in a 98% sulfuric acid solution. The molecules remained intact for weeks because the near-total absence of water prevented hydrolysis, the primary chemical reaction that usually snaps peptide bonds.

Beyond simple survival, all three peptides folded into a distinct shape known as an omega loop. Because a molecule’s physical architecture dictates how it functions, that structural stability opens up new possibilities for how complex chemistry behaves in extreme environments.

A structure that could serve a function

“Before this, people thought that peptides couldn’t survive in sulfuric acid, so showing peptides are not only stable, but also fold, is a really big deal.”

— Seager, Professor of Planetary Sciences.

Hong noted that once these molecules hold a defined three-dimensional shape, they gain the potential to perform biological functions inside acid droplets.

The discovery adds nuance to a series of experiments that have yielded mixed results. A 2024 study by members of the same research group found that dipeptides, pairs of amino acids, broke down quickly in concentrated sulfuric acid.
The new data suggests that chain length plays a critical role in molecular stability, with longer sequences offering greater resistance to chemical decay.

Independent scientists emphasize that finding folded structures in a lab dish remains distinct from discovering alien biology. Ad Bax, structural biologist, noted that while the results show protein-like shapes can endure such harsh conditions, establishing actual life on Venus still requires more evidence.

Seager’s team plans to test longer amino acid chains alongside peptide nucleic acid, a synthetic analogue to DNA, to determine if complex genetic architectures can sustain similar stress. Rather than claiming a discovery of extraterrestrial life, the researchers have simply shown that acid chemistry does not rule Venus out entirely.

Sources: MIT; Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (September 2026).
